title: From a Switch to a Thinking Machine

pages.text: A trader at Makola sells a bag of rice and is paid by mobile money. She taps her phone a few times, and within seconds the money has moved. She does not stop to wonder how. Inside that phone are billions of tiny electric circuits, switching on and off faster than anyone can imagine. Yet every one of them follows the same rule as the light switch on a classroom wall. To understand a phone, a computer, or the machines people now call artificial intelligence, begin with the simplest part of any circuit: a switch.

pages.alt: A market trader holding a mobile phone beside sacks of rice, with a customer’s phone held next to hers.

pages.text: An electric current flows only round a complete circuit. A switch is a gap in the circuit that you can close or open. Close it, and the current flows and the lamp lights: that is ON. Open it, and the current stops: that is OFF. With several switches you can make simple decisions. Put two switches in series, one after the other, and the lamp lights only if the first AND the second are closed. Put them in parallel, side by side, and it lights if one OR the other is closed. Circuits that decide like this are called logic circuits.

pages.text: The first computers, built in the 1940s, used glass tubes called valves as their switches. Valves were as big as light bulbs, became very hot, and often burned out. One early computer had about 18,000 of them and filled a large room. Then, in 1947, scientists in America invented the transistor: a switch with no moving parts, made from a material called a semiconductor and worked by a small electric signal. Transistors could be made smaller and smaller. The chip in a modern phone is the size of a fingernail and holds more than ten billion of them.

pages.text: Add a sensor to a transistor and a circuit can act without a person. Many street lights have a part whose resistance changes when light falls on it. As darkness comes, the change switches a transistor, and the lamp comes on by itself. At dawn it goes off. The same idea closes a water pump when the tank is full, sounds an alarm when there is smoke, and opens a shop door as you walk up. This is automation: machines following fixed rules that people have built in. An automatic street light is useful, but nobody would say that it thinks.

pages.text: Artificial intelligence, or AI, goes a step further. Its rules are not all written in by hand. The program is shown a huge number of examples and adjusts itself until it finds the patterns in them. That is how a phone turns speech into text, and how programs now answer questions, write essays, and translate between languages, including Twi, Ewe, and Ga. Farmers use AI apps that recognise crop diseases from a photograph of a leaf. Driverless taxis already carry passengers in a few cities abroad. All of it still runs on transistors switching ON and OFF.

pages.text: Is AI a friend or a danger? It can help doctors to read X-rays, teachers to explain, and small businesses to keep their accounts. It can also give wrong answers that sound confident, copy unfairness from the examples it learned from, produce false pictures and voices, and replace some jobs. Scientists disagree about whether machines will ever truly think, and about how risky stronger AI may become. So treat it as a tool. Check what it tells you against a trusted source. Do your own learning first. And remember that people built it, and people must decide how it is used.

activities.question: Two switches are connected in series with a lamp. When does the lamp light?
options: Only when both switches are closed

activities.question: Why did transistors replace valves?
options: Valves were too small to see
Transistors are smaller, cooler, and more reliable

activities.question: What makes an automatic street light come on at dusk?
options: A person in an office presses a switch
A sensor that responds to the fading light and switches a transistor

activities.question: Apply it: An AI program gives you an answer for your science homework. What is the wisest thing to do?
options: Copy it at once, because AI is always correct
Check it against your textbook or ask your teacher before you use it
Ignore it, because AI is always wrong

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the history of computing in order.
items: Computers are built with glass valves and fill whole rooms
Billions of transistors are packed onto a chip the size of a fingernail
Mobile phones carry a powerful computer in the pocket
AI programs answer questions and translate languages

glossary.definition: A complete loop that an electric current can flow around.
A part that opens or closes a gap in a circuit.
A tiny switch with no moving parts, worked by a small electric signal.
A material, such as silicon, that can be made to conduct or to block electric current.
A part that responds to light, heat, sound, or movement.
The use of machines that follow built-in rules without a person controlling each step.
Artificial intelligence: computer programs that learn patterns from many examples and use them to do tasks.
